title: The directory in August 2026
description: 318 listings across 26 towns. Counts, completeness and the gaps, computed from the directory itself.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
The directory numbers for August 2026, counted from the listings themselves rather than estimated. Every figure below recomputes on each build, so it is current as at the date on this article and nothing more.

## Where it stands

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Listings | 318 |
| Towns with a page | 26 |
| Towns in New South Wales | 13 |
| Towns in Victoria | 13 |
| Categories with at least one listing | 107 |
| Categories still empty | 41 |
| Listings that reach across the border | 131 |

## Completeness

Ordering on this site comes from how complete a profile is, so the interesting number is not how many listings exist but how many of them are usable.

- 288 of 318 carry a phone number, which is 91%.
- 292 carry a website.
- 157 publish opening hours, which is 49%. That is the weakest field on the directory and it is the one that decides whether a business shows up in an "open now" search.
- 290 were read from the business's own site or an official source rather than a third party listing.

The hours gap is the one worth acting on. A business with no published hours does not appear as closed, it does not appear at all, and it never finds out.

## The biggest towns

1. **Wodonga, VIC** — 165 listings
2. **Albury, NSW** — 163 listings
3. **Barnawartha, VIC** — 130 listings
4. **Jindera, NSW** — 112 listings
5. **West Wodonga, VIC** — 84 listings
6. **Baranduda, VIC** — 82 listings
7. **Tallangatta, VIC** — 82 listings
8. **Howlong, NSW** — 81 listings
9. **Lavington, NSW** — 70 listings
10. **Yackandandah, VIC** — 69 listings

## The biggest categories

2. **Wineries** — 19 listings
3. **Motels** — 18 listings
4. **Cafes** — 14 listings
5. **Mechanics** — 12 listings
6. **Bakeries** — 10 listings
7. **Restaurants** — 10 listings
8. **Walking Trails** — 7 listings
9. **Thai Restaurants** — 6 listings
10. **Parks And Gardens** — 6 listings

## What is still empty

41 categories exist in the taxonomy with nothing in them yet. A category page goes live when its first business is added, which is the same rule that applies to towns: nothing is seeded ahead of content.

If you run one of these and you are not listed, [adding a listing is free](/claim/) and stays free.

## How these numbers are produced

This article is generated from `listings.json` by `scripts/generate-wire.mjs`. There is no estimation step and no editorial pass, because there is nothing in it but arithmetic over the rows on the site. If a figure here disagrees with a category page, the category page is right and this one is older.

title: Who trades on a weekend, August 2026
description: Published Saturday and Sunday hours across 14 border towns. A count of what businesses publish, which is not the same as what they do.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Who actually publishes weekend hours across the border corridor, August 2026.

This is a count of published hours, not of availability. A business that trades Saturday and never says so is invisible to every filter that answers "open now", including this one. That gap is the point of the article.

## The table

| Town | Listings | Publish hours | Open Saturday | Open Sunday |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wodonga VIC | 165 | 80 | 34 | 14 |
| Albury NSW | 163 | 81 | 40 | 23 |
| Barnawartha VIC | 130 | 68 | 18 | 1 |
| Jindera NSW | 112 | 52 | 12 | 0 |
| West Wodonga VIC | 84 | 39 | 10 | 1 |
| Baranduda VIC | 82 | 37 | 10 | 1 |
| Tallangatta VIC | 82 | 37 | 10 | 1 |
| Howlong NSW | 81 | 37 | 10 | 1 |
| Lavington NSW | 70 | 48 | 17 | 5 |
| Yackandandah VIC | 69 | 24 | 6 | 2 |
| Chiltern VIC | 61 | 24 | 6 | 3 |
| South Albury NSW | 59 | 37 | 11 | 1 |
| Thurgoona NSW | 54 | 32 | 8 | 0 |
| North Albury NSW | 53 | 34 | 8 | 0 |

## What it shows

The column that moves most is the third one. Where a town publishes hours, the Saturday number follows. Where it does not, the town looks closed on a weekend whether it is or not.

Food and retail publish weekends without being asked. Trades mostly publish a phone number and nothing else, because a trade business does not think of its hours as a shopfront thing. Both patterns show up in the numbers above and neither is about how hard anybody works.

## If this is your business

Publishing hours, including the closed days, takes about two minutes and is the single cheapest thing that changes how often you appear. "Closed Sunday" is worth publishing: it stops a call you were never going to convert and it makes the rest of the week believable.

[Claiming a listing](/claim/) is free.

## Method

Generated by `scripts/generate-wire.mjs` from the `hours` field on listings that cover each town, whether based there or servicing it. Towns with fewer than eight listings or fewer than five publishing hours are excluded.

title: A listing without opening hours costs you calls you never hear about
description: The searches that convert are the urgent ones, and the urgent ones filter on open now. A blank hours field takes you out of the running silently.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
The most valuable search a local business gets is somebody who needs the thing right now. It is also the search where an incomplete profile costs the most, because the filtering happens before the business ever appears.

## What actually happens

Someone searching for a locksmith at 7pm is not comparing five businesses on quality. They are looking for one that is open. Every surface that answers that question, a search engine, a map, a directory, an assistant reading a page out loud, needs structured opening hours to answer it.

A business with no published hours does not appear as closed. It appears as nothing, because the filter has nothing to evaluate. The customer never sees it and the business never learns the call happened.

That is the part worth sitting with: the cost is invisible. There is no missed call in the log. There is no enquiry that went unanswered. There is a decision that was made without you in the room.

## Why closed days matter as much as open ones

"Closed Sunday" is worth publishing. It stops a call you were never going to convert, it stops a customer being annoyed at you for not answering, and it makes the rest of the hours believable.

A week with five days filled in and two blank reads as incomplete. A week with five days filled in and two marked closed reads as accurate. They contain the same information and they are not treated the same way by anything reading the page.

## Special hours are the other half

Public holidays are the single most common reason published hours are wrong, and on this border they are wrong twice as often, because [the two states do not share a calendar](/tools/public-holidays/). A Wodonga business closed for Melbourne Cup Day and an Albury business open the same day are both correct.

If you close for a holiday, say so on the listing. If you are open when everyone assumes you are shut, say that louder.

## What we do with them

Hours on this directory drive three things: the open Saturday counts in the data block on every category page, the structured data that lets a search engine answer an open now question, and the hours table on the listing itself. All three come from the same field and all three are wrong if it is empty.

Every listing shows the date its details were last read. If your hours changed since then, they are wrong on this site right now, and [correcting them](/data-and-corrections/) is free and takes a minute.

title: The Saturday problem on the border corridor
description: Weekend trade availability is thin in regional towns, and the numbers on this directory show where it is thinnest.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Most trade work in a regional town happens between 7am and 4pm on a weekday, which is exactly when most of the people who need it are at work.

That mismatch is not a complaint about tradespeople. It is a structural fact about a labour market where a business is often one or two people, and where Saturday work costs a penalty rate that a domestic customer will not always wear. But it does mean that "who is open Saturday" is one of the most useful things a directory can answer, and almost none of them do.

## What the numbers show

Every locality and category page on this site carries a count of how many listings on that page publish Saturday hours. It is computed from the hours on the listings underneath it, not estimated, and it moves as businesses claim their listings and fill in a full week.

Two patterns show up consistently across the corridor.

**Retail and food publish weekends. Trades mostly do not.** A cafe in Dean Street publishes seven days without being asked. A plumber publishes a phone number and an ABN. That is not because the plumber never works Saturday, it is because a trade business does not think of its hours as a shopfront thing.

**Emergency availability and Saturday hours are different products.** A business that takes after hours call outs is not open Saturday in any normal sense. It is contactable at a loading. Both are useful and they are not the same, so the site counts them separately.

## Why the gap exists in the data

A listing built from public sources gets hours only if the business published them. Most trade websites do not. That is the single biggest source of missing hours on this directory, and it is fixable in about two minutes by whoever owns the business.

It is also why a low Saturday count on a page is a statement about published hours, not about actual availability. The page says so.

## If you are a trade business reading this

Publishing your hours, including the days you are closed, is the cheapest thing you can do to get more of the right calls and fewer of the wrong ones. "Closed Sunday" stops a phone call at 10am Sunday that was never going to become a job.

If you take after hours work, say what triggers the loading. The number of quotes that fall over at the invoice because nobody mentioned a weekend rate is not small.

Claim the listing, add the week, done. [Here is how](/claim/).

title: How listing quality is scored, and why paid placement never moves it
description: The ordering on every results page comes from a completeness score. Here is exactly what is in it.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Every list of businesses on this site is ordered by a quality score, then by rating, then alphabetically. The score is not a secret and there is no reason for it to be one.

## What is in it

Points are awarded for the profile containing things a person searching actually needs:

- A description long enough to say what the business does
- A street address, where the business has a shopfront
- A phone number
- A website
- Opening hours, with more weight when the full week is published
- Three or more specific things the business offers
- Feature attributes, the beer garden and pet friendly and emergency call out flags
- A link to the business's Google profile
- A social account
- Details read from the business's own site rather than a third party listing
- A licence number on record

The maximum is 100. A listing below 40 is set to noindex, follow, which means it stays on the site, keeps its links, and does not go into a search index until it is worth being there.

## What is not in it

Money. There is no field on a listing that a payment writes to, and there is no branch in the ordering code that reads a payment status. That is a design decision, not a policy statement, and it is checkable: the ranking function is about ten lines long and it takes two arguments, neither of which is a plan.

Promoted placement will exist eventually. When it does it will be boxed, labelled as promoted, and excluded from the structured data that describes the results list, so a search engine reading the page is not told a paid slot is an organic result. The [advertising policy](/advertising-policy/) sets that out.

## Why completeness and not popularity

Because popularity in a regional town is mostly a function of how long a business has existed, and a directory that ranks on it is a directory that never surfaces anyone new. A five year old business with a filled in profile is more useful to somebody searching at 9pm with a burst pipe than a thirty year old one with a phone number and nothing else.

It also happens to be the only signal we can measure honestly. We do not know who is good. We do know who has published their hours.

## How to move up

Claim the listing and fill it in. It is free, it takes about ten minutes, and the score recomputes on the next build. There is no faster path and there is no paid path.

The [claim page](/claim/) explains the process.

title: What a verified badge on LocalsKnow actually means
description: It means we checked a licence number against a state register on a stated date. It is not an endorsement and it is not a guarantee.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Trust badges on directories are usually decorative. Ours is a claim about a specific action taken on a specific date, and it is worth being exact about what that claim is and is not.

## What it means

A verified badge means one thing: somebody took the licence number the business published, put it into the official register for the relevant state, and the licence came back current for the class of work the business advertises. The date of that check is shown on the listing.

That is it. That is the whole claim.

## What it does not mean

- **It is not an endorsement.** We have not used them, we have not inspected their work, and a current licence tells you nothing about whether they turn up.
- **It is not a guarantee.** A licence current in August can be suspended in September. The date on the badge is the date of the check and nothing after it.
- **It is not insurance.** Licensing and insurance are separate. Ask about insurance separately.
- **It does not cover every class of work.** A licence is for specific work. A verified general builder is not verified to do the electrical.

## What the absence of a badge means

Less than people assume. A listing without a verified badge has not been checked. That is not the same as failing a check, and it is not the same as being unlicensed.

Most listings on this site were built from public sources without the business being involved yet. Verification generally happens when an owner claims their listing and gives us a number to check. No badge usually means nobody has been through that process, not that something is wrong.

When a check is run and the licence does not come back current, the listing does not get a badge and it does not get a dofollow outbound link. We do not publish a red cross next to a business's name on the strength of a register lookup that might have a data problem in it. We contact them.

## Why the badge is tied to the outbound link

The outbound link to a business's own website is nofollow by default and becomes dofollow when the listing is claimed, complete and verified. That is deliberate, and it is the alternative to the reciprocal link arrangement the [partner program page](/partners/) explains we did not build.

A dofollow link is us vouching for a site. We are prepared to vouch for a business whose licence we checked and whose profile is filled in by its actual owner. We are not prepared to vouch for a row we scraped off a public page, however accurate that row is.

## The date is the important part

Every verified badge on this site carries the date of the check, and every listing carries the date its details were last read from a source. A badge with no date would be a claim with no expiry, which is a way of being wrong quietly for years.

If a date on a listing is old enough to bother you, treat it as old. That is what it is there for.

title: Reading a trade quote: the four lines that should be there
description: Call out, labour, materials and loadings. A quote that does not separate them is not necessarily a bad quote, but you cannot tell.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
Most complaints about trade pricing are not really about the price. They are about a number that arrived without an explanation, after the work was done.

A quote that separates four things is checkable. One that does not, is not.

## One: the call out

What it costs for someone to turn up, before any work happens. It covers the drive, the vehicle and the time.

The question that matters is whether it is waived, credited or charged on top if the job proceeds. All three arrangements are common and all three are legitimate. Finding out which one applies after the invoice arrives is the problem.

On this border, ask specifically whether travel is inside the call out or additional. A Corowa business quoting a Howlong job is driving twenty minutes each way and that time is being charged somewhere.

## Two: labour

A rate and a minimum. A one hour minimum on a domestic job is standard. Half hour increments after the first hour are common and reasonable.

What to watch: a minimum charge that is much larger than the job. A four hour minimum to change a tap is a way of saying the business does not want small jobs, which is fine, but it should be said rather than buried.

## Three: materials

Either itemised with a markup, or a single materials line. Both are normal. A markup on parts is how a trade business funds carrying stock so your hot water service gets fixed today rather than Thursday.

What to watch: materials that do not appear at all on a job that obviously used some.

## Four: loadings

After hours, weekend, public holiday, emergency. This is where the surprises live.

On the Albury Wodonga border there is a second layer, because [the two states do not share a public holiday calendar](/tools/public-holidays/). Melbourne Cup Day is a holiday rate in Wodonga and a Tuesday in Albury. Labour Day is March on one side and October on the other. A business that works both sides has two of each.

Ask what triggers a loading and what the rate is. "After hours" starting at 4pm and "after hours" starting at 6pm are different products.

## The one sentence version

If you cannot tell from the quote what you are paying for, ask before the work starts, not after. A tradesperson who will not itemise is not necessarily overcharging. You just have no way of knowing, and neither does anyone you complain to later.

Indicative ranges for common jobs are on the [what should this cost](/tools/what-should-this-cost/) page, and on every locality and category page on this site.

title: How the border changes what a tradie can legally do
description: A licence follows the work, not the ute. What that means for a Wodonga plumber on a Lavington job, and what to ask before you book.
author: The LocalsKnow desk
body:
There are about four kilometres between the middle of Albury and the middle of Wodonga. There are two separate licensing systems.

That is the single most misunderstood thing about hiring a trade on this border, and it produces the same conversation on both sides of the river every week. A customer books someone. The job goes wrong. The insurer or the tribunal asks which licence the work was done under, and nobody has a clean answer.

## The rule, stated plainly

The licence that matters is the one that applies where the work is performed. Not where the business is registered, not where the ute is garaged, not which state the ABN address says.

A plumber based in Wodonga doing a hot water replacement in Lavington is doing New South Wales work. A builder in Jindera putting up a shed in Barnawartha is doing Victorian work. The address on the invoice does not change that.

## Automatic Mutual Recognition

Since 2021 a licence holder in one state can generally work in another on the strength of their home licence, after notifying the second state's regulator, without paying a second licence fee. This is Automatic Mutual Recognition and it made the border much easier to work across than it used to be.

It did not make the border disappear. Three things are worth knowing:

- **It does not cover every occupation.** Some classes are excluded, and the exclusion lists differ between states.
- **Notification is not optional.** The scheme requires the person to notify the second state before working there. A licence holder who has not notified is not covered by it.
- **Local rules still apply.** Building permits, plumbing compliance certificates, inspection regimes and the paperwork that goes with them are set by the state the work is in. Recognition of the licence does not import the home state's process.

## What to ask

One question does most of the work: *which licence are you working under for this job, and can I have the number?*

A business that works both sides will have an answer immediately, because they field it constantly. If the answer is vague, that is the signal, not the licence number itself.

Then check it. The [licence check tool](/tools/licence-check/) goes straight to the correct register for each state.

## Why we model service area separately

Every listing on this site stores where a business is based and where it works as two different things. That is the whole reason a Wodonga operator shows up on Lavington pages, and it is also why every one of those listings carries a note saying whether the service area was stated by the business or estimated from distance.

The distinction matters here more than anywhere else in the country. "They are close enough to come" and "they are licensed to do this here" are different claims, and a directory that blurs them is not helping anyone.

More on the specifics in the guide on [NSW and VIC licence rules](/guides/nsw-vic-licence-rules/), and on [hiring a tradie on the border](/guides/hiring-a-tradie-on-the-border/).
